title: Foraging wood sorrel in UK woodland
subtitle: Identification, harvest window, and moderation guidance
excerpt: Wood sorrel is a small woodland plant with heart-shaped leaves and a sharp lemony flavour. It grows in shaded deciduous woodland from spring through early summer. Use sparingly in salads and as a garnish; the oxalic acid content means it is not a bulk vegetable.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); BSBI species accounts for Oxalis acetosella; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.

content.text: Wood sorrel (Oxalis acetosella) grows in shaded deciduous woodland and under hedgerows across the UK from spring through early summer. The small, heart-shaped leaflets fold down at night and in strong sun. The taste is sharply lemony, from oxalic acid, and works well as a garnish, in salads, and in dressings. Use in moderation; it is not suited to eating in large quantity.
: confirm (1) three heart-shaped leaflets grouped like clover, (2) a sharp lemon taste from a single leaf, and (3) the shaded woodland habitat. If any feature does not match, do not eat.
Leaves: three heart-shaped leaflets, clover-like, pale to mid-green, around 1 to 2 cm across each. They fold down flat at night.
Stems: slender, delicate, 5 to 15 cm tall. No woody stem.
Flowers (April to May): small, white with purple veins, five petals. Appear singly on thin stalks above the leaves.
Habitat: shaded deciduous woodland floor, often on mossy banks or among leaf litter.
Wood sorrel has no directly toxic

in UK woodland, but clover (Trifolium species) is sometimes confused with it. Clover leaves are oval not heart-shaped, the habitat tends to be grassland not woodland shade, and clover has no lemon taste.

Harvest from March through June, picking individual leaf groups from the stem with your fingers or scissors. Take a small pinch from several plants rather than stripping one plant bare. Wood sorrel is small and delicate; it takes quickly and regrows slowly.

Use fresh the same day; the leaves wilt within a few hours. Rinse briefly in cold water. Scatter over salads, use as a garnish on fish or egg dishes, or stir through a dressing. Cooking dulls the sharp flavour. Because of the oxalic acid content, keep portions to a small handful; people who are prone to kidney stones should avoid it entirely.

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of foliage from woodland and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Take only a small amount from any one spot; wood sorrel patches in woodland are often small and slow to recover.

rows.cause: The plant may be clover rather than wood sorrel
rows.fix: Confirm the habitat (shaded woodland, not open grassland), the leaf shape (heart-shaped, not oval), and the flavour (sharply lemony). If any feature does not match, do not eat.

rows.symptom: Leaves wilt almost immediately after picking
rows.cause: Wood sorrel is very delicate and loses moisture quickly
rows.fix: Place immediately in a damp cloth or small bag with a few drops of water. Use within two to three hours of picking.
